newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar steady in subdued Tokyo, awaits U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar steady in subdued Tokyo, awaits U.S. data.

text.p: The dollar was mostly flat against the yen and the mark in late Tokyo on Friday, with trade locked in a narrow range ahead of the release of U.S. February non-farm payroll data due at 1330 GMT.
Overnight comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin concerning a rise in Japan's current account surplus inhibited the dollar's rise, clouding its bullish outlook.
Dealers said the dollar was firmly supported by bids from Japanese investors at the 120 yen level, but many dealers agree that the dollar is vulnerable to falls in the near future.

"In the past six months or so, interest rate gaps (between Japan and the U.S.) were a major factor in pushing the dollar higher, but situation is changing and now we can't act only for that," said a dealer at a Japanese city bank.

Rubin said on Thursday that a sustained current account surplus by Japan was in "nobody's interest". His remarks came after similar remarks from U.S. officials earlier this week and Thursday's report of Japan's account account surplus.
"There is a growing fear that the U.S. may change its strong dollar policy if Japan's surplus keeps swelling," said a senior dealer at a European bank in Tokyo.
He said some Tokyo commercial operators were gradually turning bearish on long-term outlook for the dollar, following remarks by Rubin and other U.S. officials this week.

Another Japanese bank dealer said, however: "Obstacles for yen purchases are uncertainties over the Tokyo stock market and whether Japan's government can hammer out concrete steps to increase liquidity in Japan's sluggish property market within this month."
"Strong U.S. data should strengthen expectations of a U.S. credit tightening and boost the dollar/mark rate, which is interest-rate sensitive," said a bank dealer.
A dealer in Singapore said the dollar/mark had formed a base around 1.7080 after its retracement back up from near that level. "I'm looking for it to go further.
"In the short-term, 1.7250 marks should be no problem. And in the longer term, if Germany's unemployment problems continue, we could be looking at 1.7500," he said.
